A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same fixed-point-tree acceleration of generalized random forests despite changes in title and organization. All 22 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v2, including proofs, figures and v2 Appendices A–F, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulations measuring training times, tree complexity and treatment-effect estimation accuracy in Section 4 and Figures 1–5.

after.justification: v2 reports original stability experiments, simulation timings and estimation errors, plus an original California housing analysis in Section 7 and Appendix F.

M1.justification: Both versions use CART splits on Jacobian-free pseudo-outcomes followed by forest-weighted estimating equations. The one-step OLS approximation with exact line search was already described as fp2 in v1. GRF-FPT retains this procedure; expanded pseudocode and GRF implementation explanations do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: The discrete-treatment and continuous-regressor tasks remain, with the latter reframed as varying-coefficient models. v2 adds nonlinear interaction, dense logistic and random-function regimes, a correlated-regressor scenario, and geographically varying coefficient estimation on California housing data (Tables 2–3, Sections 3.2 and 7, Appendix F).

E2.justification: v1 compares grad, exact-OLS fp1 and approximate-OLS fp2. v2 reports GRF-grad versus GRF-FPT without the separate exact-OLS fp1 comparator. The original gradient baseline and previously introduced approximate fixed-point approach remain.

E3.justification: Accuracy evaluation changes from 2,000 trees, 1,000 test observations and K=2/4/8 to 100 trees, 5,000 test observations and K=4/256, with 20,000 training observations. Timing experiments expand beyond individual trees to forests of up to 1,000 trees and revise the sample-size and dimension grids (Table 1). v2 reports MSE instead of v1's normalized L2-loss presentation.

E4.justification: v2 adds a targeted robustness experiment examining split locations and variance across regressor correlations of 0.80–0.99 (Figure 1), alongside broader scaling analyses. Conversely, v1's exact-versus-approximate OLS comparison and split-count diagnostics, which tested whether acceleration resulted from simpler trees, are removed.

E5.justification: v1 documents 500 timing replications and displays their distributions; v2's timing bars omit corresponding replication counts and uncertainty displays. Accuracy replication counts change from 50 to 40. The new stability analysis reports 250 replications with median split variance and 10th/90th-percentile bands, substantially revising uncertainty reporting across the empirical evidence.

E6.justification: v2 adds or replaces extensive timing, accuracy and stability results. New housing timings are 19.1 seconds for GRF-grad versus 12.6 for GRF-FPT, a reported 1.52-fold speedup (Table 4). Accuracy is broadly similar, although the K=256 VCM Setting 2 panel shows higher FPT MSE, and some HTE timing cases favor grad. Changed protocols prevent interpreting these as same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: v2 adds an explicit asymptotic-normality theorem and regularity conditions, CART-equivalence derivations, and reasoning about honest weights' conditional independence. It substantially replaces the coupling proof, introduces child-size normalization in the fixed-point approximation, and strengthens the criterion remainder from O_P in v1 Proposition 1 to o_P in v2 Proposition 4.1.

C1.justification: The claim of faster GRF training with comparable accuracy remains. v2 additionally makes robustness to ill-conditioned Jacobians a central claimed advantage and explicitly claims reduced memory demands and computational savings scaling as O(K²) (Sections 2–3.3 and 8). These extend the contribution beyond v1's acceleration-focused framing.

C2.justification: v2 introduces a substantive explanation connecting correlated regressors, nearly singular Jacobians and smaller deep-tree nodes to unstable gradient splits. Appendix C also discusses empty honest leaves and bias in in-sample predictions. v1's interpretation that speed improvements are not explained by fewer splits is no longer developed.

D1.justification: v2 supplies author implementation and experiment/data repository links, three algorithm listings, explicit line-search and simulation-generator formulas, and housing preprocessing and fitting details (Appendices C and F). However, v1's disclosure that identical separately estimated Y.hat and W.hat values were shared across methods is no longer provided; this does not establish that the control itself changed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning within causal machine learning, varying-coefficient models, forest theory and classical fixed-point methods. Added references include Chernozhukov et al. (2018), Hastie and Tibshirani (1993), and Ryu and Boyd (2016). The explicit motivation from Yang et al. (2021) in v1 is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, background and method exposition are extensively rewritten around a Stage I/Stage II narrative. Terminology changes to GRF-FPT, detailed theory and examples move into appendices, and applications, conclusion and impact sections reshape the document's organization.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column main text and substantially redesigns the displays: timing bar-chart grids, stability plots, geographic maps, distribution plots, four tables, algorithm listings and a subsampling diagram replace or supplement v1's figures. Figure 10 also introduces a caption error reversing the dimensional labels relative to its panels.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses an important validation gap: v1 tested accuracy only through K=8 and computational gains mainly through single-tree timings. Accuracy tests at K=256, whole-forest timings, nonlinear regimes, a targeted stability experiment and real-data analysis substantially strengthen evaluation of the intended applications. Reproduction links and implementation details also improve usability. These gains outweigh the loss of exact-OLS and split-count diagnostics, although weaker timing uncertainty reporting, caption errors and overly broad interpretations of some results remain material drawbacks.
